question: How should I handle a family dispute over religious differences like the practices of Rajab?
asked: A sister argued with a relative over the hadith about the blessings of Rajab, and it has caused issues within the family. What should be done?
answer:
You see, this is actually a bigger problem than the question itself: not knowing how to deal with this issue, to the point of it causing (looks like a boycott has happened; they're not talking to one another) over an issue of an abstract nature. And this is something that we need to learn to overcome.

Suppose your cousin follows another strand of Islam, another interpretation. See, I am mainstream Sunni. I've said this from the beginning, and I'm quoting people like Ibn Taymiyyah, al-Nawawi, al-Ghazali, Ibn Hajar. These are our icons; we look up to them. But let's also recognize that there are other versions of Islam that they practice. I might not agree with it, but you cannot deny that they are there, can you? And there are people that might not agree with you. So at what point should we have an argument and break off? Definitely not over the blessings of Rajab. Definitely not.

If somebody wants to fast extra in Rajab, or even if they want to do this bizarre prayer that al-Nawawi said is a bid'ah... Okay, al-Nawawi is saying it's a bid'ah, which means other people were doing it in his time frame. I disagree with those other people; I agree with Imam al-Nawawi. But what do we do when your cousin looks up to the other group? What do we do? Do we boycott our blood and relatives? Do we have animosity with other Muslims?

Before we get to that level, before you look at the differences, first look at what you have in common, then get to the differences. Do you worship the same God? Do you face the same qiblah? Do you read the same book? Do you believe in the same Prophet? Do you want to enter the same Jannah? If all of these check, check, check, check, check, then you get to the differences. Put that difference in perspective of the commonality as well.

Please don't misunderstand. I just told you it is a bid'ah to do bizarre prayers in Rajab; I just said this. Now the second question: what do you do if your cousin insists that he or she is going to pray those prayers? Do you make them an enemy of Allah and His Messenger? Do you boycott them? Do you stop saying salam to them?

You can have a nice, gentle discussion. You can say, "Look, I'm not a scholar. I've asked the 'ulama, and they quoted me Ibn Hajar, they quoted me al-Nawawi." I just quoted you these great 'ulama: not a single authentic hadith. But they will say, "I don't know any of these names." And I'm not trying to be controversial, but they will quote Ahmad Raza Khan, saying, "That's our shaykh." Or, for the other ethnicity, they'll say, "Oh, they have Fada'il Rajab." Or another, they're going to quote this one: "This is my shaykh. I don't know your shaykh; I have my shaykh." Okay.

Can we blame this person for having an emotional connection with somebody, and not having another connection with your whole galaxy of 'ulama? In this person's mind, they've become religious by this group. They've experienced iman and zuhd and 'ibadah from a group that they know, and it's made them better people. I disagree. I'm not preaching that to you; I don't do that version of Islam. But this group does. What do we do?

We tell them, "This is our understanding," gentle, polite. If they accept, alhamdulillah. If not, they haven't committed kufr; they haven't left the fold of Islam; they're still worshipping Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala. **So don't break the ties of kinship over something that, at the end of the day, inshallah, Allah will forgive because of His rahmah.** Your cousin, your relative, is not a great 'alim or shaykh. He's an innocent Muslim, or she's an innocent Muslimah, and she's following a group that she has experienced some iman from. She's wrong in this regard, but you don't have to be judge, jury and executioner. And you don't have to treat her in a manner that... rather, if you really want to guide her, wallahi, the best way to do so, after du'a, is through your akhlaq.

And if you're going to resort to name-calling, and saying your scholars are this, and cutting off, what have you done? On the contrary, you say, "Well, okay, no problem, that's your business," and you continue having a loving relationship based upon the rahmah of our religion, based upon what it means to be the better of the two. Always be the better of the two.

And guess what? Wallahi, I have discovered this in my own life all the time. That's why I don't respond to my critics that much: because in the long run, I always find intelligence and rahmah win people of intelligence and rahmah over. And the only people that are left are people of no intelligence, or no rahmah, one of the two, or no sincerity. Otherwise, my own 25-plus years, and I've had critics of every stripe and variety: keep on doing the right thing for the right reasons with compassion. Simple as that.

And if you are consistent, the other person, guess what? They will hear from their group hatred and negativity that will shock them, like, "Oh my God." They're going to call the other group kafir and dall and mudill and sellout, and what else? All the names you've memorized. They're going to use a methodology of harshness that will demonstrate to your relative that this isn't real Islam. Not by academic arguments, because your relative is not qualified to study the chains of isnad. Your relative doesn't know what Bukhari's munkar means. Your relative does know that a simple bit of love and compassion is what our Prophet ﷺ taught. Correct? So why are you resorting to the tactics of the very group you are considering to be wrong? Show them what it means to be a real follower of the one who was sent as rahmatan lil-'alamin.

Continue the ties of kinship, have the upper hand, be gentle, forbearing, loving, and make du'a. And inshallah, at the end of the day, these trivial things are not going to cause a person to go to Jahannam or something. Even if they're mistaken, they're still within the fold of Islam. And may Allah 'azza wa jall unite you and your cousin or relative back upon the truth.
